newsitem.title: POLAND: President appoints new Polish farm minister.
newsitem.headline: President appoints new Polish farm minister.

text.p: Poland's president on Friday appointed Jaroslaw Kalinowski of the co-ruling Peasant Party (PSL) -- an advocate of protectionism in agriculture -- as the new farming minister.

Kalinowski, whose more liberal-minded predecessor was ousted in April following pressure from his PSL party, pledged new measures to protect the farm market and said preparation for tough accession talks with the European Union was his priority.

"Measures will be taken to protect our market more efficiently ...They will be compatible with our international agreements," Kalinowski, 35, told reporters after President Aleksander Kwasniewski named him.

Kalinowski, whose term in office will last until soon after general elections around September, said Poland should negotiate its EU membership carefully to secure the best possible position in the union.
"The time of negotiations is most important, perhaps even more important than the entry date, because our position in the EU will depend on it," he said.
Poland hopes to begin EU entry negotiations early in 1998 and join soon after the year 2000.
Its outmoded agriculture -- where some 30 percent of the workforce is employed, compared with an average of less than five percent in the EU -- is seen as a major hurdle for Poland's entry.
EU officials say Kalinowski and his successors face a radical reform involving cutting the number of farms to less than one million from the current more than two million.
Kalinowski declined to go into details on his view on the reform, saying only that he supported family-owned, European-style farms.

He vowed immediate steps to help Polish potato and hops growers by imposing higher customs duties in these sectors. He also said rampant alcohol smuggling must stop or local distilleries would see a further decline in profits.

Kalinowski was also named to be one of three deputy prime ministers as envisaged by a power-sharing agreement governing the coalition of the Peasants and the bigger, ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) party.
His candidacy was pushed through by the Peasant leader, Waldemar Pawlak, who represents mostly small farm owners keen to uphold state protection of agriculture.

Kalinowski's predecessor, Roman Jagielinski, leader of the more market-oriented faction in the Peasant Party, lost the confidence of the party leadership after he unsuccessfully challenged Pawlak for their group's presidency last year.
Pawlak and most other senior Peasants accused Jagielinski of policies resulting in a food trade deficit last year and low grain prices for domestic farmers.

Many analysts dismissed these allegations as unfounded and suggested the attack on Jagielinski was designed to help the party in the eyes of farm voters by distancing it from the government's record before elections.
